Burmese Translation

## The Book of the Elevens
## 1. Nissaya Vagga
## 1. Kimatthiya Sutta
1. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, and after approaching and paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side. Sitting at one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of skillful virtues?" "Ānanda, the purpose of skillful virtues is freedom from remorse (avippaṭisāra), and their benefit is freedom from remorse."
"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of freedom from remorse?" "Ānanda, the purpose of freedom from remorse is joy (pāmojja), and its benefit is joy."
"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of joy?" "Ānanda, the purpose of joy is rapture (pīti), and its benefit is rapture."
"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of rapture?" "Ānanda, the purpose of rapture is tranquility (passaddhi), and its benefit is tranquility."
"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of tranquility?" "Ānanda, the purpose of tranquility is happiness (sukha), and its benefit is happiness."
"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of happiness?" "Ānanda, the purpose of happiness is concentration (samādhi), and its benefit is concentration."
"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of concentration?"
516:
"Ānanda, the purpose of concentration is the knowledge and vision of things as they really are (yathābhūtañāṇadassana), and its benefit is the knowledge and vision of things as they really are."
"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of the knowledge and vision of things as they really are?" "Ānanda, the purpose of the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is disenchantment (nibbidā), and its benefit is disenchantment."
"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of disenchantment?" "Ānanda, the purpose of disenchantment is dispassion (virāga), and its benefit is dispassion."
"Venerable Sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of dispassion?" "Ānanda, the purpose of dispassion is the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana), and its benefit is the knowledge and vision of liberation."
"Thus, Ānanda, skillful virtues have freedom from remorse as their purpose and benefit; freedom from remorse has joy as its purpose and benefit; joy has rapture as its purpose and benefit; rapture has tranquility as its purpose and benefit; tranquility has happiness as its purpose and benefit; happiness has concentration as its purpose and benefit; concentration has the knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its purpose and benefit; the knowledge and vision of things as they really are has disenchantment as its purpose and benefit; disenchantment has dispassion as its purpose and benefit; dispassion has the knowledge and vision of liberation as its purpose and benefit. Thus, Ānanda, skillful virtues lead step by step to the highest (arahantship)."
The First Sutta.
## 2. Cetanākaraṇီya Sutta
2. "Monks, for one who is virtuous and possessed of virtue, there is no need for an act of will (cetanā) such as: 'May freedom from remorse arise in me.' It is in the nature of things (dhammatā), monks, that freedom from remorse arises in one who is virtuous and possessed of virtue."
"Monks, for one who is free from remorse, there is no need for an act of will such as: 'May joy arise in me.' It is in the nature of things, monks, that joy arises in one who is free from remorse."
"Monks, for one who is joyful, there is no need for an act of will such as: 'May rapture arise in me.' It is in the nature of things, monks, that rapture arises in one who is joyful."
"Monks, for one who has a rapturous mind, there is no need for an act of will such as: 'May my body be tranquil.' It is in the nature of things, monks, that the body becomes tranquil for one who has a rapturous mind."
"Monks, for one whose body is tranquil, there is no need for an act of will such as: 'I shall experience happiness.' It is in the nature of things, monks, that one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness."
517:
Monks, for one who is happy, there is no need for an act of will: 'May my mind be concentrated.' It is the nature of things, monks, that the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. Monks, for one who is concentrated, there is no need for an act of will: 'May I know and see things as they really are.' It is the nature of things, monks, that one who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are. Monks, for one who knows and sees things as they really are, there is no need for an act of will: 'May I be disenchanted.' It is the nature of things, monks, that one who knows and sees things as they really are becomes disenchanted. Monks, for one who is disenchanted, there is no need for an act of will: 'May I be dispassionate.' It is the nature of things, monks, that one who is disenchanted becomes dispassionate. Monks, for one who is dispassionate, there is no need for an act of will: 'May I realize liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation.' It is the nature of things, monks, that one who is dispassionate realizes liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

In this way, monks, dispassion has the knowledge and vision of liberation as its purpose and benefit. Disenchantment has dispassion as its purpose and benefit. Knowing and seeing things as they really are has disenchantment as its purpose and benefit. Concentration has knowing and seeing things as they really are as its purpose and benefit. Happiness has concentration as its purpose and benefit. Tranquility has happiness as its purpose and benefit. Rapture has tranquility as its purpose and benefit. Joy has rapture as its purpose and benefit. Freedom from remorse has joy as its purpose and benefit. Wholesome virtues have freedom from remorse as their purpose and benefit. In this way, monks, states flow into states, states fulfill states, for the purpose of going from this shore of the round of suffering to the far shore (Nibbāna).

The Second Sutta.

## 3. First Upanisā Sutta

3. Monks, for one who is immoral, whose virtue has failed, the proximate cause for freedom from remorse is destroyed. When there is no freedom from remorse, for one who lacks freedom from remorse, the proximate cause for joy is destroyed. When there is no joy, for one who lacks joy, the proximate cause for rapture is destroyed. When there is no rapture, for one who lacks rapture, the proximate cause for tranquility is destroyed. When there is no tranquility...
518:
...for one who lacks tranquility, the proximate cause for happiness is destroyed. When there is no happiness, for one who lacks happiness, the proximate cause for concentration is destroyed. When there is no concentration, for one who lacks concentration, the proximate cause for knowing and seeing things as they really are is destroyed. When there is no knowing and seeing things as they really are, for one who lacks knowing and seeing things as they really are, the proximate cause for disenchantment is destroyed. When there is no disenchantment, for one who lacks disenchantment, the proximate cause for dispassion is destroyed. When there is no dispassion, for one who lacks dispassion, the proximate cause for the knowledge and vision of liberation is destroyed.

Monks, just as for a tree that is deficient in branches and foliage, the outer bark does not come to fullness, nor the inner bark, nor the sapwood, nor the heartwood. In the same way, monks, for one who is immoral, whose virtue has failed, the proximate cause for freedom from remorse is destroyed. When there is no freedom from remorse, for one who lacks freedom from remorse, the proximate cause for joy is destroyed. ...p... up to the knowledge and vision of liberation being destroyed.

Monks, for one who is virtuous, whose virtue is complete, the proximate cause for freedom from remorse is fulfilled. When there is freedom from remorse, for one who possesses freedom from remorse, the proximate cause for joy is fulfilled. When there is joy, for one who possesses joy, the proximate cause for rapture is fulfilled. When there is rapture, for one who possesses rapture, the proximate cause for tranquility is fulfilled. When there is tranquility, for one who possesses tranquility, the proximate cause for happiness is fulfilled. When there is happiness, for one who possesses happiness, the proximate cause for right concentration is fulfilled. When there is right concentration, for one who possesses right concentration, the proximate cause for knowing and seeing things as they really are is fulfilled. When there is knowing and seeing things as they really are, for one who possesses knowing and seeing things as they really are, the proximate cause for disenchantment is fulfilled. When there is disenchantment, for one who possesses disenchantment, the proximate cause for dispassion is fulfilled. When there is dispassion, for one who possesses dispassion, the proximate cause for the knowledge and vision of liberation is fulfilled.

Monks, just as for a tree that is complete in branches and foliage, the outer bark comes to fullness, the inner bark, the sapwood, and the heartwood. In the same way, monks, for one who is virtuous, whose virtue is complete, the proximate cause for freedom from remorse is fulfilled. When there is freedom from remorse, for one who possesses freedom from remorse, the proximate cause for joy is fulfilled. ...p... up to the knowledge and vision of liberation being fulfilled.

The Third Sutta.

## 7. Paṭhama Saññā Sutta

7. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, could a monk obtain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth, nor percipient of water in water, nor percipient of fire in fire, nor percipient of air in air, nor percipient of the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, nor percipient of the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness, nor percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, nor percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor percipient of this world in this world, nor percipient of the other world in the other world, nor percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought, or pondered by the mind—and yet he would be percipient?”

“Ānanda, a monk could obtain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth, nor percipient of water in water, nor percipient of fire in fire, nor percipient of air in air, nor percipient of the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, nor percipient of the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness, nor percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, nor percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,”
523:
“One would not be percipient of this world in this world, nor would one be percipient of the other world in the other world. One would not be percipient of whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or explored by the mind; yet, one would still be percipient.” (Thus the Blessed One said.)

“Venerable sir, how could a bhikkhu attain such a concentration where he would not be percipient of earth in earth, nor percipient of water in water, nor percipient of fire in fire, nor percipient of air in air? Where he would not be percipient of the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, nor percipient of the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness, nor percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, nor percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? Where he would not be percipient of this world in this world, nor percipient of the other world in the other world? Where he would not be percipient of whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or explored by the mind; yet, he would still be percipient?”

“Ānanda, here a bhikkhu is percipient thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu could attain such a concentration where he would not be percipient of earth in earth, nor percipient of water in water, nor percipient of fire in fire, nor percipient of air in air; nor percipient of the base of infinite space... nor percipient of the base of infinite consciousness... nor percipient of the base of nothingness... nor percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... nor percipient of this world in this world, nor percipient of the other world in the other world. He would not be percipient of whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or explored by the mind; yet, he would still be percipient.”
524:
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging friendly and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Sāriputta:

“Friend Sāriputta, could a bhikkhu attain such a concentration where he would not be percipient of earth in earth... [as before]... nor percipient of whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or explored by the mind; yet, he would still be percipient?”

“Friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu could attain such a concentration where he would not be percipient of earth in earth... [as before]... nor percipient of whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or explored by the mind; yet, he would still be percipient.”

“But how, friend Sāriputta, could a bhikkhu attain such a concentration...?”

“Friend Ānanda, here a bhikkhu is percipient thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ In this way, friend Ānanda, a bhikkhu could attain such a concentration where he would not be percipient of earth in earth... [as before]... nor percipient of whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or explored by the mind; yet, he would still be percipient.”

“It is wonderful, friend! It is marvelous, friend! How the meaning and the phrasing of the Teacher and the disciple coincide and agree, and do not diverge, regarding the highest point! Just now, friend, I approached the Blessed One and asked him about this matter. The Blessed One explained this matter to me with these same words, these same phrases, and these same expressions, just as the Venerable Sāriputta has done. It is wonderful, friend! It is marvelous, friend! How the meaning and the phrasing of the Teacher and the disciple coincide and agree, and do not diverge, regarding the highest point!”

The seventh sutta.

## 8. Manasikāra Sutta

8. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, could a bhikkhu not attend to the eye, not attend to forms, not attend to the ear, not attend to sounds,”

...should not attend to the nose, should not attend to odors, should not attend to the tongue, should not attend to tastes, should not attend to the body, should not attend to tangibles, should not attend to earth, should not attend to water, should not attend to fire, should not attend to air, should not attend to the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), should not attend to the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana), should not attend to the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), should not attend to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), should not attend to this world, should not attend to the other world; and yet, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—even that he should not attend to, and yet he should be attentive? Is it possible, Bhante, for a bhikkhu to attain such a state of concentration?"

"It is possible, Ānanda, for a bhikkhu to attain such a state of concentration where he should not attend to the eye, should not attend to forms, should not attend to the ear, should not attend to sounds, should not attend to the nose, should not attend to odors, should not attend to the tongue, should not attend to tastes, should not attend to the body, should not attend to tangibles, should not attend to earth, should not attend to water, should not attend to fire, should not attend to air, should not attend to the sphere of infinite space, should not attend to the sphere of infinite consciousness, should not attend to the sphere of nothingness, should not attend to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, should not attend to this world, should not attend to the other world; and yet, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—even that he should not attend to, and yet he should be attentive."

"But how, Bhante, is it possible for a bhikkhu to attain such a state of concentration where he should not attend to the eye, should not attend to forms... [p] ...and yet, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—even that he should not attend to, and yet he should be attentive?"

In this way, Ānanda, it is possible for a bhikkhu to attain such a state of concentration where he should not attend to the eye, should not attend to forms... [p]"
