## 9. Saddha Sutta

9. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nātika in the Brick House. Then the Venerable Saddha approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Saddha:

"Saddha, meditate like a thoroughbred horse; do not meditate like an inferior horse. And what, Saddha, is the meditation of an inferior horse? An inferior horse, Saddha, tied at the feeding trough, meditates, 'Fodder, fodder.' Why is that? Because, Saddha, it does not occur to the inferior horse tied at the feeding trough: 'What task will the horse trainer have me do today? What should I do in return for him?' Tied at the feeding trough, it just meditates, 'Fodder, fodder.'

In the same way, Saddha, an inferior man here, whether gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, dwells with a heart overcome by sensual lust, obsessed by sensual lust. He does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. Harboring sensual lust within, he meditates, over-meditates, out-meditates, and mis-meditates. He dwells with a heart overcome by ill will. He dwells with a heart overcome by sloth and torpor. He dwells with a heart overcome by restlessness and remorse. He dwells with a heart overcome by doubt, obsessed by doubt. He does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. Harboring doubt within, he meditates, over-meditates, out-meditates, and mis-meditates.

He meditates dependent on earth, he meditates dependent on water, he meditates dependent on fire, he meditates dependent on air, he meditates dependent on the sphere of infinite space, he meditates dependent on the sphere of infinite consciousness, he meditates dependent on the sphere of nothingness, he meditates dependent on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he meditates dependent on this world, he meditates dependent on the other world; and whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—he meditates dependent on that too. This, Saddha, is the meditation of an inferior man.

And how, Saddha, is the meditation of a thoroughbred horse? A good thoroughbred horse, Saddha, tied at the feeding trough, does not meditate, 'Fodder, fodder.' Why is that? Because, Saddha, it occurs to the good thoroughbred horse tied at the feeding trough: 'What task will the horse trainer have me do today?"
527:
“...thinking, ‘What task will the horse-trainer have me do today? How shall I respond to him?’ That thoroughbred horse tied to the trough does not think, ‘Fodder, fodder.’ Sandha, that thoroughbred horse regards the application of the goad as a debt, as a bond, as a loss, as a misfortune.

In the same way, Sandha, a thoroughbred man who has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, does not dwell with a mind obsessed by sensual desire, nor is he overwhelmed by sensual desire. He understands as it really is the escape from arisen sensual desire. He does not dwell with a mind obsessed by ill will... by sloth and torpor... by restlessness and remorse... by doubt, nor is he overwhelmed by doubt. He understands as it really is the escape from arisen doubt. He does not meditate depending on earth, nor depending on water, nor depending on fire, nor depending on air, nor depending on the base of the infinity of space (ākāsānañcāyatana), nor depending on the base of the infinity of consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana), nor depending on the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), nor depending on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), nor depending on this world, nor depending on the world beyond. Whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—on that too he does not meditate dependingly. And yet, he does meditate. Sandha, when a thoroughbred man meditates in this way, the gods including Indra, Brahmā, and Pajāpati worship him even from afar, saying:

‘Homage to you, O thoroughbred man!
Homage to you, O supreme man!
We do not understand that
depending on which you meditate.’

When this was said, the Venerable Sandha said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable Sir, in what way does a thoroughbred man meditate so that he does not meditate depending on earth, nor depending on water, nor depending on fire, nor depending on air, nor depending on the base of the infinity of space, nor depending on the base of the infinity of consciousness, nor depending on the base of nothingness, nor depending on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor depending on this world, nor depending on the world beyond, nor depending on whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—and yet, he does meditate?’
528:
‘Venerable Sir, in what way does a thoroughbred man meditate so that the gods including Indra, Brahmā, and Pajāpati worship him even from afar, saying: “Homage to you, O thoroughbred man! Homage to you, O supreme man! We do not understand that depending on which you meditate”?’

‘Sandha, here for a thoroughbred man, the perception of earth in regard to earth is dispelled; the perception of water in regard to water is dispelled; the perception of fire in regard to fire is dispelled; the perception of air in regard to air is dispelled; the perception of the base of the infinity of space in regard to the base of the infinity of space is dispelled; the perception of the base of the infinity of consciousness in regard to the base of the infinity of consciousness is dispelled; the perception of the base of nothingness in regard to the base of nothingness is dispelled; the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in regard to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is dispelled; the perception of this world in regard to this world is dispelled; the perception of the world beyond in regard to the world beyond is dispelled; and the perception in regard to whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind is also dispelled. Sandha, a thoroughbred man who meditates in this way does not meditate depending on earth... (as before) ...nor depending on whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—and yet, he does meditate (on Nibbāna through the attainment of fruition). Sandha, when a thoroughbred man meditates in this way, the gods including Indra, Brahmā, and Pajāpati worship him even from afar, saying:

“Homage to you, O thoroughbred man!
Homage to you, O supreme man!
We do not understand that
depending on which you meditate.”’

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Moranivāpa Sutta

10. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Moranivāpa (Peacocks' Feeding Ground), the park of the wanderers. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: ‘Bhikkhus.’ ‘Venerable Sir,’ those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses three qualities is one who has reached the absolute goal, the absolute security from bondage, the absolute holy life, the absolute end; he is the best among devas and humans.’
529:
What are the three? They are the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekha), the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, and the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training. Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities is one who has reached the absolute goal, the absolute security from bondage, the absolute holy life, the absolute end, and is supreme among devas and humans.

Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with another three qualities is one who has reached the absolute goal, the absolute security from bondage, the absolute holy life, the absolute end, and is supreme among devas and humans. What are the three? They are the miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya), the miracle of telepathy (ādesanāpāṭihāriya), and the miracle of instruction (anusāsanīpāṭihāriya). Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities is one who has reached the absolute goal, the absolute security from bondage, the absolute holy life, the absolute end, and is supreme among devas and humans.

Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with another three qualities is one who has reached the absolute goal, the absolute security from bondage, the absolute holy life, the absolute end, and is supreme among devas and humans. What are the three? They are right view, right knowledge, and right liberation (the fruition of Arahantship).

Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities is one who has reached the absolute goal, the absolute security from bondage, the absolute holy life, the absolute end, and is supreme among devas and humans. Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with two qualities is one who has reached the absolute goal, the absolute security from bondage, the absolute holy life, the absolute end, and is supreme among devas and humans. What are the two? They are knowledge (vijjā) and conduct (caraṇa). Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with these two qualities is one who has reached the absolute goal, the absolute security from bondage, the absolute holy life, the absolute end, and is supreme among devas and humans. Monks, this verse was spoken by Brahma Sanaṅkumāra:

'The Khattiya is the best among those people who value lineage,
But one endowed with knowledge and conduct is the best among devas and humans.'

Monks, that verse spoken by Brahma Sanaṅkumāra was well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it is beneficial, not unbeneficial; and it is approved by me.
530:
It is not ill-spoken; it is beneficial, not unbeneficial; and I approve of it. Monks, I also say the same:

'The Khattiya is the best among those people who value lineage,
But one endowed with knowledge and conduct is the best among devas and humans.'

The tenth sutta.
The first chapter, the Nissaya Vagga, is finished.

## 2. Anussati Vagga
## 1. Pathama Mahānāma Sutta

11. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park. At that time, many bhikkhus were making a robe for the Blessed One, thinking: 'When the robe is finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour.' Mahānāma the Sakyan heard that many bhikkhus were making a robe for the Blessed One, thinking: 'When the robe is finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour.'

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, I have heard this: "Many bhikkhus are making a robe for the Blessed One, thinking: 'When the robe is finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour.'" Venerable sir, for us who live in various ways, in what way should we live?'

'Good, good, Mahānāma! It is fitting for clansmen like you to approach the Tathāgata and ask: "Venerable sir, for us who live in various ways, in what way should we live?" Mahānāma, one with faith succeeds (in attaining the paths and fruits), not one without faith. One with aroused energy succeeds, not one who is lazy. One with established mindfulness succeeds, not one who is forgetful. One who is concentrated succeeds (in attaining the paths and fruits).'
531:
One who is not concentrated cannot succeed. One who is wise can succeed [in attaining the Path and Fruit]; one who is not wise cannot succeed. Mahānāma, being established in these five things, you should further develop six things.

Mahānāma, here you should recollect the Tathāgata: 'Thus is the Blessed One: an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.' Mahānāma, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, his mind is not overwhelmed by lust, nor by hatred, nor by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight, with the Tathāgata as the object. Mahānāma, a noble disciple with a straight mind gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. In one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness. In one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. Mahānāma, this noble disciple is said to dwell in equanimity among a generation that is restless (with lust, hatred, and delusion), to dwell without anxiety among a generation that is anxious, and having entered the stream of Dhamma, he develops the recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati-bhāvanā).

Furthermore, Mahānāma, you should recollect the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.' Mahānāma, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma, his mind is not overwhelmed by lust, nor by hatred, nor by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight, with the Dhamma as the object. Mahānāma, a noble disciple with a straight mind gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. In one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness. In one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. Mahānāma, this noble disciple is said to dwell in equanimity among a generation that is restless...
532:
...to dwell without anxiety among a generation that is anxious, and having entered the stream of Dhamma, he develops the recollection of the Dhamma (Dhammānussati-bhāvanā).

Furthermore, Mahānāma, you should recollect the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing uprightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing rightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing properly. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples—the four pairs of persons, the eight [types of] individuals—is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.'

Mahānāma, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha, his mind is not overwhelmed by lust, nor by hatred, nor by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight, with the Saṅgha as the object. Mahānāma, a noble disciple with a straight mind gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. In one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness. In one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. Mahānāma, this noble disciple is said to dwell in equanimity among a generation that is restless, to dwell without anxiety among a generation that is anxious, and having entered the stream of Dhamma, he develops the recollection of the Saṅgha (Saṅghānussati-bhāvanā).

Furthermore, Mahānāma, you should recollect your own virtues: virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unspotted, unblemished, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. Mahānāma, at the time when a noble disciple recollects his virtue, his mind is not overwhelmed by lust, nor by hatred, nor by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight, with virtue as the object. Mahānāma, a noble disciple with a straight mind gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. In one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness. In one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. Mahānāma, this noble disciple is said to dwell in equanimity among a generation that is restless, to dwell without anxiety among a generation that is anxious.
533:
He is said to have entered the stream of Dhamma and to be developing the meditation on the recollection of virtue (sīlānussatibhāvanā).

Furthermore, Mahānāma, [you should reflect]: 'It is a gain for me, it is a great gain for me, that in a population obsessed by the stain of stinginess, I dwell at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, with clean hands, delighting in giving, one to be asked, delighting in sharing and distributing gifts.' Thus you should recollect your own generosity (cāga).

Mahānāma, when a noble disciple recollects generosity, his mind is not obsessed by lust, not obsessed by hatred, and not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is upright, based on generosity. Mahānāma, a noble disciple with an upright mind gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is glad, rapture is born; for one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil; one with a tranquil body feels happiness; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, Mahānāma, is called a noble disciple who dwells in harmony among a discordant population, who dwells without affliction among an afflicted population, who has entered the stream of Dhamma and develops the recollection of generosity (cāgānussatibhāvanā).

Furthermore, Mahānāma, you should recollect the deities: 'There are the Devas of the Four Great Kings, the Devas of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Devas, the Tusita Devas, the Devas who Delight in Creation, the Devas who Wield Power over the Creations of Others, the Devas of the Brahma-group, and deities beyond these. Those deities, possessed of such faith that when they passed away from here they were reborn there, such faith is also found in me. Those deities, possessed of such virtue... such learning... such generosity... such wisdom that when they passed away from here they were reborn there, such wisdom is also found in me.' Thus you should repeatedly recollect the deities [taking them as witnesses to your own qualities of faith and so forth].

Mahānāma, when a noble disciple recollects the faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom of both himself and those deities, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, not obsessed by hatred, and not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is upright, based on the deities [taking them as witnesses to his own qualities]. Mahānāma, a noble disciple with an upright mind gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is glad, rapture is born; for one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil; one with a tranquil body feels happiness; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, Mahānāma, is called a noble disciple who dwells in harmony among a discordant population...
534:
...who dwells without affliction among an afflicted population, who has entered the stream of Dhamma and develops the recollection of deities (devatānussatibhāvanā).

First Sutta.

## 2. Second Mahānāma Sutta

12. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park. At that time, Mahānāma the Sakyan had recovered from an illness, not long after his recovery. At that time, many bhikkhus were making a robe for the Blessed One, [thinking]: 'When the robe is finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour.'

Mahānāma the Sakyan heard: 'Many bhikkhus, it is said, are making a robe for the Blessed One; when the robe is finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour.' Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, I have heard this: "Many bhikkhus are making a robe for the Blessed One; when the robe is finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour." Venerable sir, for us who live in various ways, in what way should we live?'

'Good, good, Mahānāma! It is fitting for you clansmen to approach the Tathāgata and ask: "Venerable sir, for us who live in various ways, in what way should we live?" Mahānāma, one with faith is an achiever, not one without faith. One with aroused energy is an achiever, not one who is lazy. One with established mindfulness is an achiever, not one who is forgetful. One who is concentrated is an achiever, not one who is unconcentrated. One with wisdom is an achiever, not one who is unwise. Mahānāma, established in these five qualities, you should further develop six qualities.

Mahānāma, here you should recollect the Tathāgata: "It is for this reason that the Blessed One is... [etc.]... teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."

Mahānāma, when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust...'
535:
his mind is not overwhelmed by hatred, his mind is not overwhelmed by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight, based on the Tathāgata. Mahānāma, the noble disciple whose mind is straight gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. For one who is glad, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. Mahānāma, you should develop this recollection of the Buddha while walking, while standing, while sitting, while lying down, while busy at work, and while living in a home crowded with children.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, you should recollect the Dhamma... [p]... the Saṅgha... [p]... your own virtue... [p]... your own generosity... [p]... you should recollect the deities: 'There are the deities of the Four Great Kings... [p]... there are deities higher than that. Those deities, possessed of such faith, passed away from here and were reborn there; such faith is also found in me. Those deities, possessed of such virtue... learning... generosity... wisdom, passed away from here and were reborn there; such wisdom is also found in me.' Thus, you should repeatedly recollect the deities (using them as witnesses to your own qualities such as faith).

Mahānāma, at the time when the noble disciple repeatedly recollects the faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom of both himself and those deities, at that time his mind is not overwhelmed by lust, his mind is not overwhelmed by hatred, his mind is not overwhelmed by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight, based on the deities (using them as witnesses to his own qualities). Mahānāma, the noble disciple whose mind is straight gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. For one who is glad, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. Mahānāma, you should develop this recollection of the deities while walking, while standing, while sitting, while lying down, while busy at work, and while living in a home crowded with children.

The second sutta.

## 3. Nandiya Sutta

13. At one time, the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodhārāma monastery. At that time, the Blessed One intended to enter the rains retreat at Sāvatthī. Nandiya the Sakyan heard the report: "The Blessed One, it is said, intends to enter the rains retreat at Sāvatthī."
536:
Then it occurred to Nandiya the Sakyan: "What if I too were to enter the rains retreat at Sāvatthī? There I can attend to my work and also get to see the Blessed One from time to time."

Then the Blessed One entered the rains retreat at Sāvatthī. Nandiya the Sakyan also entered the rains retreat at Sāvatthī. There he attended to his work and also got to see the Blessed One from time to time. At that time, many monks were making robes for the Blessed One, thinking: "When the robes are finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour."

Nandiya the Sakyan heard the report: "Many monks, it is said, are making robes for the Blessed One, thinking that when the robes are finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour." Then Nandiya the Sakyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down at one side. Sitting there, Nandiya the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I have heard this: 'Many monks are making robes for the Blessed One, thinking that when the robes are finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour.' Venerable Sir, for us who live in various ways, in what way should we dwell?"

"Good, good, Nandiya! It is proper for you clansmen, Nandiya, to approach the Tathāgata and ask: 'Venerable Sir, for us who live in various ways, in what way should we dwell?' Nandiya, one who has faith is one who succeeds, not one who is faithless. One who has virtue is one who succeeds, not one who is immoral. One who has aroused energy is one who succeeds, not one who is lazy. One who has established mindfulness is one who succeeds, not one who is forgetful. One who is concentrated is one who succeeds, not one who is unconcentrated. One who has wisdom is one who succeeds, not one who is unwise. Nandiya, established in these six qualities, you should develop mindfulness internally in five things.

"Here, Nandiya, you should recollect the Tathāgata: 'The Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed...'
537:
‘He is the Teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’ In this way, Nandiya, you should establish mindfulness internally with reference to the Tathāgata.

“Furthermore, Nandiya, you should recollect the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, onward leading, and to be realized by the wise for themselves.’ In this way, Nandiya, you should establish mindfulness internally with reference to the Dhamma.

“Furthermore, Nandiya, you should recollect your good friends: ‘It is a gain for me, it is a great gain for me, that I have good friends who are compassionate, desiring my welfare, who advise and instruct me.’ In this way, Nandiya, you should establish mindfulness internally with reference to good friends.

“Furthermore, Nandiya, you should recollect your own generosity: ‘It is a gain for me, it is a great gain for me, that in a population obsessed by the stain of stinginess, I dwell at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, delighting in giving and sharing.’ In this way, Nandiya, you should establish mindfulness internally with reference to generosity.

“Furthermore, Nandiya, you should recollect the devas: ‘There are devas who, having transcended the company of devas who subsist on solid food, have been reborn in a certain mind-made body; they do not see anything further to be done for themselves, nor an accumulation of what has been done. Just as, Nandiya, a bhikkhu who is liberated in a way that is not temporary does not see anything further to be done for himself, nor an accumulation of what has been done; even so, Nandiya, those devas who, having transcended the company of devas who subsist on solid food, have been reborn in a certain mind-made body, do not see anything further to be done for themselves, nor an accumulation of what has been done.’ In this way, Nandiya, you should establish mindfulness internally with reference to the devas.

“Nandiya, a noble disciple possessed of these eleven factors indeed abandons evil unwholesome states and does not cling to them. Just as, Nandiya, an overturned pot vomits out water and does not take back what has been vomited; or just as, Nandiya, when a fire is let loose in a dry grass-thicket, it only goes forward burning and does not [return to] what is already burnt,”
538:
“...return to what is already burnt; even so, Nandiya, a noble disciple possessed of these eleven factors indeed abandons evil unwholesome states and does not cling to them.”

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Subhūti Sutta

14. Then the Venerable Subhūti, together with a monk named Saddha, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As the Venerable Subhūti was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Subhūti, what is the name of this monk?”

“Venerable Sir, this monk is named Saddha. He is the son of the lay follower Sudatta (Anāthapiṇḍika) and has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith.”

“But Subhūti, does this monk Saddha, the son of the lay follower Sudatta, who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, manifest the characteristics of a faithful person?”

“Now is the time, Blessed One; now is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to speak about the characteristics of a faithful person for Saddha. Now I shall know whether this monk manifests the characteristics of a faithful person or not.”

“Then listen, Subhūti, and pay close attention; I will speak.”

“Yes, Venerable Sir,” the Venerable Subhūti replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Here, Subhūti, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken the rules of training, he trains in them. That a bhikkhu is virtuous... and trains in the rules of training—this, Subhūti, is a characteristic of a faithful person.

“Furthermore, Subhūti, a bhikkhu is learned, a sustainer of what he has heard, a storehouse of learning. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings he has much heard, retained, recited, mentally investigated, and fully penetrated by view. That a bhikkhu is learned... and fully penetrated by view—this too, Subhūti, is a characteristic of a faithful person.

“Furthermore, Subhūti, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, and good associates.”
539:
...is inclined towards good friends. Subhūti, that a monk has good friends, good companions, and is inclined towards good friends—this too, Subhūti, is a mark of faith in one who has faith.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a monk is easy to speak to, endowed with qualities that make him easy to admonish, patient, and receives instruction respectfully. Subhūti, that a monk is easy to speak to, endowed with qualities that make him easy to admonish, patient, and receives instruction respectfully—this too, Subhūti, is a mark of faith in one who has faith.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a monk is skillful and tireless in the various duties, whether great or small, to be done for his fellow monks, inquiring "What should be done?"; he is endowed with investigative wisdom regarding the means to carry them out, and is capable of acting and organizing.

Subhūti, that a monk is skillful and tireless in the various duties, whether great or small, to be done for his fellow monks, inquiring "What should be done?", being endowed with investigative wisdom regarding the means to carry them out, and being capable of acting and organizing—this too, Subhūti, is a mark of faith in one who has faith.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a monk is a lover of the Dhamma, pleasant in conversation, and feels great joy in the excellent Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya. Subhūti, that a monk is a lover of the Dhamma, pleasant in conversation, and feels great joy in the excellent Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya—this too, Subhūti, is a mark of faith in one who has faith.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not neglect the duty of cultivating wholesome states. Subhūti, that a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states, being steadfast, firm in effort, and not neglecting the duty of cultivating wholesome states—this too, Subhūti, is a mark of faith in one who has faith.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a monk obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life. Subhūti, that a monk obtains at will the four jhānas which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life...
540:
...without difficulty or trouble—this too, Subhūti, is a mark of faith in one who has faith.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a monk recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-destruction, many aeons of world-evolution, many aeons of world-destruction and evolution: "In such a birth, I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn in such a birth; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn here." Thus, with their aspects and details, he recollects his manifold past lives. Subhūti, that a monk recollects his manifold past lives... etc. ...this too, Subhūti, is a mark of faith in one who has faith.

Furthermore, Subhūti, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses that of human beings, a monk sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma:

"Friends, these beings were endowed with bad conduct of body (kāyaduccarita), bad conduct of speech (vacīduccarita), and bad conduct of mind (manoduccarita). They reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell. But these beings were endowed with good conduct of body (kāyasucarita), good conduct of speech (vacīsucarita), and good conduct of mind (manosucarita). They did not revile the noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right views. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, even in a heavenly world." Thus, he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. In this way, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses that of human beings, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. Subhūti, that a monk with the divine eye... etc. ...understands how beings fare according to their kamma—this too, Subhūti, is a mark of faith in one who has faith.
541:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, with the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind [Arahatship] and liberation by wisdom [Arahatship], and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. This too, Subhūti, is a mark of faith in one who has faith."

When this was said, the Venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, those marks of faith in one who has faith spoken of by the Blessed One are found in this bhikkhu, and this bhikkhu is seen to possess them.

Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara), seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken the rules of training, he trains in them.

Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu is learned, a sustainer of what he has heard, a storehouse of what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings have been much heard by him, retained, recited, mentally pondered, and well penetrated by view.

Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, good associates.

Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu is easy to admonish... respectfully accepts instruction.

Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu is skillful and tireless in the various duties to be done for his fellow monks, whether great or small, inquiring 'What should be done?'; he is possessed of investigative wisdom as to the means, able to do them and able to arrange them.

Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu is a lover of the Dhamma, pleasant in conversation, filled with noble joy in the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Abhivinaya.

Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused... strong, firm in exertion, not casting off the duty regarding wholesome states.

Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu obtains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas, which belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life."
542:
"...obtains them without trouble or difficulty. Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their modes and details. Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu, with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), which is purified and surpasses that of human beings... understands beings according to their kamma. Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu, with the destruction of the taints... realizes and dwells. Venerable Sir, those marks of faith in one who has faith spoken of by the Blessed One are found in this bhikkhu, and this bhikkhu is seen to possess them."

"Good, good, Subhūti! Therefore, Subhūti, you should dwell together with this faithful bhikkhu. And whenever you, Subhūti, wish to see the Tathāgata, you should approach to see the Tathāgata together with this faithful bhikkhu."

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Mettā Sutta

15. "Bhikkhus, when the liberation of mind by loving-kindness (mettā cetovimutti) has been pursued, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and properly perfected, eleven benefits may be expected. What eleven? One sleeps happily. One wakes happily. One does not see bad dreams. One is dear to human beings. One is dear to non-human beings (devas, animals, spirits). Deities protect one. Fire, poison, and weapons do not affect one. The mind is easily concentrated. The facial complexion is bright. One dies unconfused. If one does not penetrate further [to Arahatship], one goes to the Brahma world.

Bhikkhus, when the liberation of mind by loving-kindness has been pursued, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and properly perfected, these eleven benefits may be expected."

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta

16. On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in Beluva village.

At that time, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business.
543:
Then Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanagara approached a certain monk at the Kukkuṭārāma monastery and said to him: "Venerable sir, where is the venerable Ānanda staying now? We wish to see the venerable Ānanda." The monk replied, "Householder, the venerable Ānanda is staying at the village of Beluvagāmaka in Vesālī."

Then Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanagara, having finished his business in Pāṭaliputta, approached the venerable Ānanda at Beluvagāmaka in Vesālī. Having approached and paid homage to the venerable Ānanda, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanagara said to the venerable Ānanda:

"Venerable Ānanda, is there one single Dhamma proclaimed by the Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One—whereby a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, can liberate his unliberated mind, or his unexhausted taints can reach exhaustion, or he can attain the unsurpassed security from bondage that he has not yet attained?"

"There is, householder, one single Dhamma proclaimed by the Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One—whereby a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, can liberate his unliberated mind, or his unexhausted taints can reach exhaustion, or he can attain the unsurpassed security from bondage that he has not yet attained."

"And what, venerable Ānanda, is that one single Dhamma proclaimed by the Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One—whereby a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, can liberate his unliberated mind, or his unexhausted taints can reach exhaustion, or he can attain the unsurpassed security from bondage that he has not yet attained?"

"Here, householder, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. He reflects thus: 'This first jhāna is conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.' He understands this. Standing on that, he attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then because of that desire for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous rebirth, attaining Nibbāna there, not liable to return from that world."
544:
"Householder, this too is one single Dhamma proclaimed by the Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One—whereby a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, can liberate his unliberated mind, or his unexhausted taints can reach exhaustion, or he can attain the unsurpassed security from bondage.

Furthermore, householder, with the subsiding of initial and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without initial and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. ... [He enters and dwells in] the third jhāna ... the fourth jhāna. He reflects thus: 'This jhāna is conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.' He understands this. Standing on that, he attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then because of that desire for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous rebirth, attaining Nibbāna there, not liable to return from that world.

Householder, this too is one single Dhamma proclaimed by the Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One—whereby a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, can liberate his unliberated mind, or his unexhausted taints can reach exhaustion, or he can attain the unsurpassed security from bondage.

Furthermore, householder, a monk dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. He reflects thus: 'This liberation of mind through loving-kindness is conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.' He understands this.

Standing on that, he attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then because of that desire for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous rebirth, attaining Nibbāna there."
545:
He is one who does not return from that world. "Householder, this dharma too has been known [by the Blessed One]... [pe]... he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been attained."

"Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion... [pe]... with a mind imbued with appreciative joy... [pe]... with a mind imbued with equanimity; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. He reflects thus: 'This liberation of mind through equanimity is conditioned and volitionally produced.' He understands: 'Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Standing on that [attainment], he reaches the destruction of the taints. If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then through that very lust for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world. Householder, this dharma too has been known by that Blessed One... [pe]... he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been attained."

"Furthermore, householder, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of infinite space is conditioned and volitionally produced.' He understands: 'Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Standing on that, he reaches the destruction of the taints. If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then through that very lust for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world. Householder, this dharma too has been known by that Blessed One... [pe]... he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been attained."

"Furthermore, householder, by completely surmounting the base of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite,' a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness... [pe]... by completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing,' he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of nothingness is conditioned and volitionally produced.' He understands: 'Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Standing on that, he reaches the destruction of the taints."
546:
"If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then through that very lust for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world. Householder, this dharma too has been known [by the Blessed One]... [pe]... he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been attained."

When this was said, Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara said to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, just as if a man seeking a single opening to a treasure trove were to find eleven openings to treasure troves all at once; even so, venerable sir, while seeking a single door to the Deathless, I have at once received eleven doors to the Deathless to attend to. Venerable sir, just as if a man had a house with eleven doors, and if that house were on fire, he could save himself through any one of those doors; even so, venerable sir, I will be able to save myself through any one of these eleven doors to the Deathless. Venerable sir, these followers of other sects seek a teacher's fee for their teacher; why then should I not perform a puja for the venerable Ānanda?"

Then Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara, having assembled the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from Vesālī and Pāṭaliputta, served and satisfied them with his own hands with choice food, both hard and soft. He presented each bhikkhu with a pair of cloths, and he presented the venerable Ānanda with a set of three robes. He also had a monastery worth five hundred [kahāpaṇas] built for the venerable Ānanda.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Gopāla Sutta

17. "Bhikkhus, a cowherd possessed of eleven factors is incapable of tending a herd of cattle and making it prosper. What are the eleven? Here, bhikkhus, a cowherd is not one who knows forms, is not skilled in characteristics, does not remove fly-eggs, does not dress wounds, does not smoke out [pests], does not know the ford, does not know what has been drunk, does not know the path, is not skilled in pastures, milks dry, and does not pay extra honor to the bulls who are the fathers and leaders of the herd. Bhikkhus, a cowherd possessed of these eleven factors is incapable of tending a herd of cattle and making it prosper."
547:
Monks, in the same way, a monk possessed of eleven qualities is incapable of achieving growth, increase, and expansion in this Dhamma-Vinaya. What are the eleven? Monks, in this teaching, a monk does not know forms, is not skilled in signs, does not remove fly-eggs, does not dress wounds, does not make smoke, does not know the ford, does not know what has been drunk, does not know the path, is not skilled in pastures, milks to the dregs, and does not pay extra respect to the elder monks of long standing, who have been ordained for a long time, who are the fathers of the Saṅgha and leaders of the Saṅgha.

And how, monks, does a monk not know forms? Monks, in this teaching, a monk does not understand as it really is all forms, namely: 'The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.' In this way, monks, a monk does not know forms. (1)

And how, monks, is a monk not skilled in signs? Monks, in this teaching, a monk does not understand as it really is: 'A fool is characterized by his actions; a wise man is characterized by his actions.' In this way, monks, a monk is not skilled in signs. (2)

And how, monks, does a monk not remove fly-eggs? Monks, in this teaching, a monk tolerates an arisen thought of sensual desire (kāmavitakka); he does not abandon it, dispel it, eliminate it, or bring it to an end. [He tolerates] an arisen thought of ill-will (byāpādavitakka)... an arisen thought of cruelty (vihiṃsāvitakka)... he tolerates whatever evil unwholesome states arise; he does not abandon them, dispel them, eliminate them, or bring them to an end. In this way, monks, a monk does not remove fly-eggs. (3)

And how, monks, does a monk not dress wounds? Monks, in this teaching, having seen a form with the eye, a monk grasps at its signs and features. Since evil unwholesome states of covetousness (abhijjhā) and displeasure (domanassa) might invade one who dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained, he does not practice for its restraint; he does not guard the eye-faculty, nor does he achieve restraint over the eye-faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear... Having smelled an odor with the nose... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue... Having felt a tactile object with the body... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he grasps at its signs and features...
548:
...he grasps at its signs and features. Since evil unwholesome states of covetousness (abhijjhā) and displeasure (domanassa) might invade one who dwells with the mind-faculty unrestrained, he does not practice for its restraint; he does not guard the mind-faculty, nor does he achieve restraint over the mind-faculty. In this way, monks, a monk does not dress wounds. (4)

And how, monks, does a monk not make smoke? Monks, in this teaching, a monk does not teach the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it and as he has learned it. In this way, monks, a monk does not make smoke. (5)

And how, monks, does a monk not know the ford? Monks, in this teaching, a monk does not from time to time approach those monks who are very learned, experts in the scriptures, who remember the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Matikas, and ask them: 'Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?' Those venerable ones do not reveal to him what is hidden, do not clarify what is obscure, and do not dispel his doubts about various doubtful points of the Dhamma. In this way, monks, a monk does not know the ford. (6)

And how, monks, does a monk not know what has been drunk? Monks, in this teaching, when the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a monk does not gain an understanding of the meaning, does not gain an understanding of the Dhamma, and does not gain the joy connected with the Dhamma. In this way, monks, a monk does not know what has been drunk. (7)

And how, monks, does a monk not know the path? Monks, in this teaching, a monk does not understand as it really is the Noble Eightfold Path. In this way, monks, a monk does not know the path. (8)

And how, monks, is a monk not skilled in pastures? Monks, in this teaching, a monk does not understand as it really is the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). In this way, monks, a monk is not skilled in pastures. (9)

And how, monks, does a monk milk to the dregs? Monks, in this teaching, faithful householders invite a monk to accept robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. In that case, the monk does not know moderation in accepting. In this way, monks, a monk milks to the dregs. (10)
549:
“Monks, how is a monk one who does not honor those elder monks of long standing, long ordained, who are fathers of the Saṅgha and leaders of the Saṅgha, with extra respect? Here, monks, a monk does not maintain deeds of loving-kindness by body, speech, or mind towards those elder monks of long standing, long ordained, who are fathers of the Saṅgha and leaders of the Saṅgha, both openly and in private. Thus, monks, a monk is one who does not honor those elder monks of long standing, long ordained, who are fathers of the Saṅgha and leaders of the Saṅgha, with extra respect. (11)

Monks, a monk endowed with these eleven factors is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and expansion in this Dhamma-Vinaya.

Monks, a cowherd endowed with eleven factors is fit to look after and increase the herd of cattle. What are the eleven? Here, monks, a cowherd knows forms, is skilled in signs, removes fly eggs, covers wounds, makes smoke, knows the ford, knows what is drunk, knows the path, is skilled in pastures, milks with a remainder, and honors with extra respect those bulls who are the fathers and leaders of the herd. Monks, a cowherd endowed with these eleven factors is fit to look after and increase the herd of cattle. In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with eleven factors is fit to attain growth, increase, and expansion in this Dhamma-Vinaya. What are the eleven? Here, monks, a monk knows forms, is skilled in signs, removes fly eggs, covers wounds, makes smoke, knows the ford, knows what is drunk, knows the path, is skilled in pastures, milks with a remainder, and honors with extra respect those elder monks of long standing, long ordained, who are fathers of the Saṅgha and leaders of the Saṅgha.

Monks, how does a monk know forms? Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is any form whatsoever as: ‘The four great elements and form derived from the four great elements.’ Thus, monks, a monk knows forms. (1)

Monks, how is a monk skilled in signs? Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: ‘A fool is characterized by his actions; a wise man is characterized by his actions.’ Thus, monks, a monk is skilled in signs. (2)”
550:
“Monks, how does a monk remove fly eggs? Here, monks, a monk does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, makes an end of it, and leads it to non-existence. He does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will... an arisen thought of cruelty... he does not tolerate any arisen evil unwholesome states; he abandons them, dispels them, makes an end of them, and leads them to non-existence. Thus, monks, a monk removes fly eggs. (3)

Monks, how does a monk cover wounds? Here, monks, on seeing a form with the eye, a monk does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the eye-faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might invade him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the eye-faculty, he achieves restraint of the eye-faculty. On hearing a sound with the ear... On smelling an odor with the nose... On tasting a flavor with the tongue... On touching a tangible with the body... On cognizing a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the mind-faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might invade him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the mind-faculty, he achieves restraint of the mind-faculty. Thus, monks, a monk covers wounds. (4)

Monks, how does a monk make smoke? Here, monks, a monk teaches the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard and learned it. Thus, monks, a monk makes smoke. (5)

Monks, how does a monk know the ford? Here, monks, from time to time, a monk approaches those monks who are learned, heirs to the tradition, experts on the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Mātikās, and inquires: ‘How is this, venerable sir? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerable ones reveal to him what was hidden, clarify what was obscure, and dispel his doubts on various points of doubt. Thus, monks, a monk knows the ford. (6)

Monks, how does a monk know what is drunk? Here, monks, when the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a monk gains understanding of the meaning,”
551:
...he gains an understanding of the Dhamma, he gains joy connected with the Dhamma. In this way, monks, a monk knows the drink. (7)

How, monks, does a monk know the path? Here, monks, a monk understands the Noble Eightfold Path (Ariya Aṭṭhaṅgika Magga) as it really is. In this way, monks, a monk knows the path. (8)

How, monks, is a monk skilled in the pasture? Here, monks, a monk understands the four foundations of mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna) as they really are. In this way, monks, a monk is skilled in the pasture. (9)

How, monks, is a monk one who milks with a remainder? Here, monks, lay followers with faith invite a monk with robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. In that case, the monk knows moderation in receiving. In this way, monks, a monk is one who milks with a remainder. (10)

How, monks, is a monk one who honors with extra honor those monks who are elders, of long standing, long ordained, fathers of the Saṅgha, and leaders of the Saṅgha? Here, monks, a monk maintains bodily acts of loving-kindness towards those monks who are elders, of long standing, long ordained, fathers of the Saṅgha, and leaders of the Saṅgha, both openly and in private; he maintains verbal acts of loving-kindness... he maintains mental acts of loving-kindness towards them both openly and in private. In this way, monks, a monk is one who honors with extra honor those monks who are elders, of long standing, long ordained, fathers of the Saṅgha, and leaders of the Saṅgha. (11)

Monks, a monk possessed of these eleven qualities is capable of achieving growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Vinaya.

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Pathama Samādhi Sutta

18. Then many monks approached the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, sat down to one side. Sitting there, those monks said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, could a monk attain such a state of concentration (samādhi) that he would not be percipient of earth in earth, not be percipient of water in water, not be percipient of fire in fire, not be percipient of air in air, not be percipient of the base of the infinity of space in the base of the infinity of space, not be percipient of the base of the infinity of consciousness in the base of the infinity of consciousness, not be percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness,
552:
not be percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, not be percipient of this world in this world, not be percipient of the other world in the other world; and also not be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, and explored by the mind—and yet he would still be percipient?"

"Monks, a monk could attain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth... [pe] ...and yet he would still be percipient."

"But, Venerable Sir, how could a monk attain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth... [pe] ...and yet he would still be percipient?"

"Here, monks, a monk is percipient in this way: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' In this way, monks, a monk could attain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth, not be percipient of water in water, not be percipient of fire in fire, not be percipient of air in air, not be percipient of the base of the infinity of space in the base of the infinity of space, not be percipient of the base of the infinity of consciousness in the base of the infinity of consciousness, not be percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, not be percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, not be percipient of this world in this world, not be percipient of the other world in the other world; and also not be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, and explored by the mind—and yet he would still be percipient."

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Dutiya Samādhi Sutta

19. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks!" "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One.
553:
The Blessed One said this: "Monks, could a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth, nor be percipient of water in water... [etc.] ...nor be percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, nor be percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor be percipient of this world in this world, nor be percipient of the world beyond in the world beyond; and also not be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—and yet he would be percipient?"

"Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it."

"Then listen, monks, and attend closely; I will speak." "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Monks, a bhikkhu could attain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth... [etc.] ...and also not be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—and yet he would be percipient."

"But in what way, venerable sir, could a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth... [etc.] ...and also not be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—and yet he would be percipient?"

"Here, monks, a bhikkhu is percipient thus: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' In this way, monks, a bhikkhu could attain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth... [etc.] ...and also not be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—and yet he would be percipient."

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Tatiya Samādhi Sutta

[etc.] ...and also not be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—and yet he would be percipient?"

[etc.] ...and also not be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—and yet he would be percipient."

The Tenth Sutta.

## 11. Catuttha Samādhi Sutta

21. There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, could a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration that he would not be percipient of earth in earth, nor be percipient of water in water, nor be percipient of fire in fire, nor be percipient of air in air, nor be percipient of the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, nor be percipient of the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness, nor be percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, nor be percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor be percipient of this world in this world, nor be percipient of the world beyond in the world beyond; and also not be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—
555:
(But) they asked: "Could there be the attainment of such a concentration (samādhi) where one would still be percipient?"

"Friends, we have come from afar to the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if the meaning of this statement occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta himself. Having heard it from the Venerable Sāriputta, the bhikkhus will remember it."

"Then, friends, listen and attend closely; I will speak."

"Yes, friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

"Friends, there could be such an attainment of concentration for a bhikkhu where he would not be percipient of earth in earth... [etc.] ...nor would he be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind; and yet he would still be percipient."

"But, friend, how could there be such an attainment of concentration for a bhikkhu where he would not be percipient of earth in earth... [etc.] ...nor would he be percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind; and yet he would still be percipient?"

"Here, friends, a bhikkhu is percipient thus: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' In this way, friends, there could be such an attainment of concentration for a bhikkhu where he would not be percipient of earth in earth, nor percipient of water in water, nor percipient of fire in fire, nor percipient of air in air, nor percipient of the base of the infinity of space in the base of the infinity of space, nor percipient of the base of the infinity of consciousness in the base of the infinity of consciousness, nor percipient of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, nor percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor percipient of this world in this world, nor percipient of the other world in the other world, nor percipient of what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind; and yet he would still be percipient."
556:
And yet he would still be percipient.

Eleventh Sutta.
The second chapter, the Anussati Vagga, is finished.
